en: Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Brahman, who is the sole object of devotion to be accomplished through one's own duty, knowledge, and dispassion, is proclaimed in the Gītā scripture.
The two-fold culmination, consisting of knowledge and action, characterized by yoga and well-refined,
was taught in the first hexad for the purpose of accomplishing the realization of the Self.
In the middle [path], for the sake of attaining the true nature of the Lord's reality,
the yoga of devotion (bhaktiyoga), which is accomplished through both knowledge and action, is proclaimed.
The discrimination between primordial matter (pradhāna), the individual self (puruṣa), the manifest (vyakta), and the Lord of all (sarveśvara)—
consisting of action, wisdom, devotion, and so forth— is the final [topic] mentioned, which remains as a supplement to what preceded.
Aiming at Pārtha, who was distressed by misplaced affection, compassion, and the notions of dharma and adharma, this non-wounding instruction of the scripture has been composed. (Yogasūtra-bhāṣya 5)
The wisdom of Sāṃkhya and Yoga has as its sphere of action the eternal Self, non-attachment, and action;
it is described in the second chapter as the mark of one whose intellect is steady, for the sake of pacifying that delusion.

In the third chapter, it is stated that action is to be performed without attachment for the sake of protecting the world, by attributing agency to the qualities (guṇas) or by consigning it to the Lord of All.
In the fourth chapter, as a consequence, the description of the true nature of action and its non-action,
the distinctions of knowledge, and its greatness are declared.
The ease and swiftness of karma-yoga, certain types of it, and the method for attaining knowledge of Brahman are taught in the fifth chapter. (Yogasūtra 9)
The method for practicing yoga, the fourfold yogi, the means of accomplishing yoga, the perfected state of yoga, and the sixth is said to be the supremacy of one's own yoga. (Yogasūtra 10)

One's own true nature, the concealment by primordial nature (prakṛti), taking refuge, the classification of devotees, and the preeminence of the awakened one—these are said to be the seven topics. (Yogasūtra 11)

In the eighth division, the true nature of sovereignty and the imperishable is declared for those seeking the feet of the Blessed One, as well as the state of what is to be known and what is to be adopted.
In the ninth chapter, one's own greatness in human form and the supreme nature of the Great-Souled Ones are proclaimed; therein, yoga is celebrated in the form of devotion.

The tenth [chapter] described in detail is intended for the arising and increase of devotion, consisting of the realization that one's own infinite auspicious qualities are entirely under one's own control. YGAS 14.
In the eleventh [chapter], there is the presentation of the direct perception of his true nature; likewise, it is stated that devotion is the sole means for both knowledge and attainment. YGAS 15.

The excellence of devotion, the teaching on the means, the state of being established in the Self for one who is incapable [of other paths], its varieties, and extreme love for the devotee—these twelve are proclaimed. (Yogasūtra-bhāṣya 16)
The true nature of the body, the means of attaining the Self, the purification of the Self, and discernment regarding the cause of bondage—these thirteen are proclaimed. (Yogasūtra 3.17)

Their agency in the process of binding by the qualities (guṇas), the cessation thereof, and the fact that the three states of existence are rooted in themselves—these fourteen [topics] are proclaimed. (Yogasūtra-bhāṣya 18)

From the unmixed and pure consciousness, the Supreme Person is declared to be distinct by virtue of his pervasive activity, his sustaining power, and his lordship; thus he is said to be the fifteenth.

The sixteenth [chapter] is taught for the sake of establishing firmness in the knowledge of the practice of reality, preceded by the exposition of the division between the gods and the asuras, and the subjection to the scriptures.

The entire non-scriptural [path] is demonic, while that which conforms to scripture is distinct by virtue of its qualities; thus, the definition of what is established by scripture has been declared in three ways as seventeenfold. YGAS 21.
The notion of agency in God, the acceptance of *sattva* as the means, and finally,
the transformation of one's own karma— this is said to be the essential meaning of the scriptures.
The yoga of action consists of the practice of austerity, pilgrimage, charity, sacrifice, and so forth;
the yoga of knowledge is the abiding in the perfectly pure self by those who have conquered their inner minds.
Bhaktiyoga is the state of remaining in meditation and other practices through the love of supreme single-minded devotion;
furthermore, there is a mutual integration of all three yogas by means of these three.

And for the obligatory and occasional rites, which consist of the propitiation of the Supreme, these three are also means of accomplishment by way of yoga for the purification of the self. (Yogasūtra-bhāṣya 2.1.25)
Having cast off all ignorance and perceived the Self as following after the Supreme, and having attained supreme devotion, he reaches that state by means of that very devotion. (Yogasūtra 26)
If one seeks that [Brahman], the yoga of devotion is the means for attaining complete sovereignty;
if one seeks the Self, all three of these are the means for achieving that absolute liberation.
For these qualified practitioners, their single-minded devotion to the Blessed One is equal;
yet, if they seek the supreme goal, they attain that very state eternally until its fulfillment.
But the man of knowledge is supremely devoted, his very self and life dependent on Him;
his sole pleasure and pain consist in union with and separation from Him, and his intellect is fixed on Him alone. (Yogasūtrabhāṣya 29)

Having attained self-mastery through the practice of meditation on the Blessed One, through utterances, salutations, praises, and hymns of glory, his life-force, mind, intellect, senses, and activities become entirely directed toward Him.

One should perform [the rites] from "one's own karma" (nijakarma) up to "devotion" (bhakti), being impelled solely by love; having abandoned the notion of it being a means, one should fearlessly entrust that [agency] to the Lord.
One who finds sole delight in exclusive and ultimate servitude shall attain that state;
this scripture has that as its primary purpose—such is the summary of the meaning of the Gītā. (Yogasūtra-bhāṣya 32)
